## The Omar slop story

> Demonstrates: blunt narrative, real stakes, plain words, no polish, lands the emotional turn without announcing it.

A great story for this is my friend Omar. He worked with a company and paid them a decent amount of money to review something in his funnel. What he got back was genuinely AI slop. It was not truly about him. It was a mess, crappy, and got sent over anyway. He basically said, never again will I ever trust them. I will never give them money. It genuinely hurt him. Not because the money was much for him, but because they outsourced the thing that made them important, likable, usable, and trustworthy. Now they were not trustworthy.

## Aim for 90 percent

> Demonstrates: direct second person, short declaratives, names the standard, ends on the creator's responsibility.

With AI content, do not aim for perfection. Aim for 90 percent done. You are what makes you unique, so your eyes need to be on it. It needs to sound like you. It needs to be how you explain stuff. The source needs to come from you. AI can brainstorm with you, but you need to be the one leading.

## Don't make a mega skill

> Demonstrates: contrarian setup, plain mechanism, the "master of all trades and master of none" turn, no jargon.

Do not make a mega skill. People like to put together one skill that is supposed to be the whole SOP or workflow. It sounds amazing to have one skill that writes the hook, call to actions, segments, stories, end hooks, titles, and thumbnails. But what happens is it becomes master of all trades and master of none, so the results are sub-par.

## Make it pull from your brain dump

> Demonstrates: the frustration named plainly, the "fraud" gut-punch, his actual cadence.

Make AI pull from your brain dump and build the content from that. Doing it the other way around, where AI comes up with the brain dump and then you correct it, is frustrating. Now you are trying to correct somebody else's words and make them sound like yours. It makes you a fraud.
